problem_data.story:
THE SILENT VALLEY
BY PATRICIA GRAHAM

One little region couldn't have a monopoly on all the communication breakdowns in the world. They did, though!

They say artificial intelligence creates opportunities, especially if "they" are trying to keep their own job of selling AI systems. I know the CommPredict made one peculiar mess of a job for me, the unpleasantly complex results of which are still lingering with me.

Xavier Hicks, my boss at Global-Meridian Communications, beamed over the sprawling neural network's holographic displays and quantum processors as proudly as if he had just personally invented it. "This will simplify your job to the point of a pleasant diversion, Sharma."

"Are you going to keep paying me for staying with my little hobby?" I asked, suspiciously eyeing my silicon competitor.

"The CommPredict poses no threat to your career. It will merely keep you from flying off on wild-goose chases. It will unvaryingly separate from the vast body of legitimate network failures the suspicious ones they try to spike us for. Then all that remains is for you to gather the accessory details, the evidence to document our erring clients."

"Fine," I said. I didn't bother to inform him that that was all my job had ever been.

Xavier shuffled his data cards. They were cards for the machine, listing new individual cases of network disruption across our continental fiber-optic grid. Since the two-month-old machine was literate and could read standard formats, the cards weren't coded or specially formatted. He read the top one. "Now this, for instance. No network analyst need investigate this outage. The circumstances obviously are such that no suspicious pattern could exist. Of course, the brain will make an unfailing analysis of all the factors involved and clear the case automatically and officially."

Xavier threaded the single card into the slot for an example to me. He then activated the interface and we stood there watching the monster ruminate thoughtfully. It finally chimed and spit the card back at Global-Meridian's top junior vice-president.

He took it like a man.

"That's what the machine is for," he said philosophically. "To detect human error. Hmm. What kind of reading do you get out of this?"

He handed me the rejected analysis card. I took it, finding a new, neatly typed notation on it. It said:

Investigate the Oakridge village of Lakeside Village.

"You want me to project it in a movie theater and see how it stands all alone in the dark?" I asked.

"Just circle up the wagon train and see how the Indians fall," Xavier said anxiously.

"It's too general. What does the silicon-brained machine mean by investigating a whole village? I don't know if it has corrupted routers, illegal signal jammers, or a hideout for corporate espionage. I don't care much either. It's not my business. How could a whole village be causing systematic network failures?"

"Find that out," he said. "I trust the machine. There have been cases of coordinated interference before. Until you get back, we are making no more installations in that settlement."

Research. To a writer that generally means legally permissible plagiarism. For a network analyst, it means earnest work.

Before I headed for the hills, or the Oakridge Region, I walked a few hundred feet down the hall and into the manual record files. The brain abstracted from empirical data but before I flew out to Lakeside Village I had to find the basis for a few practical, nasty suspicions.

Four hours of flipping switches and looking at holographic projections while a dark-haired technician in a standard uniform carried me data modules to order gave me only two ideas. Neither was very original. The one that concerned business was that the whole village of Lakeside Village must be communication-cursed.

I rejected that one almost immediately. While a communication blackout in one location was itself a statistical anomaly, the idea of a whole village of them gathered together stretched the fabric of reality to the point where even information theory couldn't help it.

There was an explanation for the recent rise in the network failure rate down there. The crystal mine there had gone into high-level operation. I knew why from the equipment, terminals, data centers, and server farms across the region. They were all using crystalline processors. The boom in quantum-grade crystals for information processing eclipsed earlier periods of silicon, graphene, and optical systems completely. The distinctive grade of crystal from Lakeside Village was being put into use all over the planet and in the orbital stations on the Moon and Mars.

Yet the rise in network failures, compared to the rise in production, was out of all proportion.

Furthermore, the work at the mine could hardly explain the excessive communication disruption reports we had had from the village as far back as our records went.

We had documented most of the failures since they seemed irrefutably genuine. All were complete with diagnostic reports and authenticated circumstances.

There was one odd note in the pattern: We had never had a report of any kind of wireless communication failure from Lakeside Village—only wired connections failed.

I shut off the projector and nodded my thanks to the technician. She brushed dark hair from her face and gave me a tired smile—she'd been on shift for hours helping me dig through those records.

It may be best to keep an open mind, but I have found in practice that you have to have some kind of working theory which you must proceed to prove is either right or wrong.

Tentatively, I decided that for generations the citizens of Lakeside Village had been in an organized conspiracy to sabotage Global-Meridian and its predecessors of hundreds upon hundreds of thousands of dollars in false network claims and replacement equipment.

Maybe they made their whole livelihood off us before the mine opened up.

I used my pocket comm and had my assistant get me a flight reservation and authorization for field investigation.

After so many profitable decades, Lakeside Village wasn't going to take kindly to my spoil-sport interference.

The hypersonic flight to Pearlbrook was smooth and relatively fast. Despite atmospheric turbulence we managed Mach 2.1 most of the way. My particular flight attendant introduced herself as Anna, a pleasant young woman working the premium cabin. The businessman in the next pod was already monopolizing his own attendant's attention—a woman with dark curly hair who seemed to tolerate his demands with professional grace. He was the type who took the service for granted and aimed to get his money's worth.

Anna returned with my beverage, and I noticed her hair caught the cabin light with a copper gleam as she leaned down. She mentioned she was majoring in Organizational Development in her night courses. I didn't have much time to get acquainted or more than hear the outline of her thesis on the corporate governance structures affected by venture capital funding. 

I gave her a smile and began flipping through the data files in my briefcase as we decelerated for a landing at Greater Oakridge. She came by once more to collect my empty glass, that distinctive auburn shade again catching my eye—it reminded me of autumn leaves, the same color as my sister's before she'd gone gray.

It took me a full five minutes to find out that I couldn't take a shuttle to Lakeside Village. Something about magnetic interference in the mountains.

Since that put me back in the days of ground transport, I arranged for a rental vehicle at the terminal. I selected an all-terrain model that could handle the mountain roads. The drive would be tedious but necessary.

It was a tiresome forty-mile drive, on manual all the way after I left the automated highway system of the city. Up and down, adjusting for curves, shifting modes for the hills.

The whole trip hardly seemed worth it when I saw the cluster of prefabricated buildings that was Lakeside Village. They looked like a tumble of modular housing units tossed in front of a massive crystalline outcropping. That was Crystal Peak in the near foreground. But I remembered that over the course of some forty years the people in these few little structures had cost Global-Meridian three quarters of a billion credits.

I turned off onto the gravel road, the sound system alerting me to the change in surface. Then I stepped down hard on my brakes, bracing myself against the safety harness. I had almost struck an old woman sitting at the side of the road, wrapped in weather-worn clothing.

"Are you okay?" I yelled, opening the window.

"I've suffered no harm at your hands—or your vehicle, miss. But I could use some help," the old woman said. "Could I trouble you for a ride when you leave town?"

I wasn't too sure about that. Most of these people who are wandering around talking like they owned advanced degrees besides their basic education belonged to some cult or other. I try to be as tolerant as I can, and some of my best friends are eccentric, but I don't want to drive with them down lonely mountain roads.

"We'll see what we can work out," I said. "Right now can you tell me where I can find Director Bruno Salazar?"

"I can," she said. "But you will have to walk there."

"Okay. It shouldn't be much of a walk in Lakeside Village."

"It's the building at the end of the path."

"It is," I said. "Why shouldn't I drive up there? The road's open."

The old woman stared at me with tired eyes. "Director Salazar doesn't like people to run vehicles with electronic systems on the paths of Lakeside Village."

"So I'll just lock the vehicle up and walk over there. I couldn't go getting tire tracks all over your clean paths."

The old woman watched as I climbed down and secured the vehicle.

"You would probably damage your systems if you did drive here, you know," she said conversationally.

"Well," I said, "I'll be getting along." I tried to walk sideways so I could keep an eye on her.

"Come back," she said, as if she had doubts.

The signs of a menacing conspiracy were growing stronger, I felt. I had my authorization codes inside my jacket, but I decided I might need a less formal means of expression. Without breaking stride, I picked up a small sample of the bluish crystal from the roadside and slipped it into my equipment pocket.

I have made smarter moves in my time.

As I approached the building at the end of the path, I saw it was about the most haphazard construction job I had seen in my life. It looked as architecturally secure as a child's drawing of a home. The angles were measurably out of line. Around every joint were misaligned seams and poorly sealed connections. The surface coating was spotty and streaked. Half the windows had visible cracks. I fought down the concern in my mind, afraid of the structural integrity of the place.

My foot caught on the top step and I nearly crashed face first into the front door. I had been too busy looking at the building, I decided. I knocked.

Moments later, the door opened.

The lean-faced man who greeted me had his hair uncombed and his shirt buttoned incorrectly. But his eyes were bright and alert.

"Are you Mr. Bruno Salazar, the liaison for Global-Meridian Communications?" I put to him.

"I'm the director, name of Salazar. But you ain't the first to formalize my title. You from the company?"

"Yes," I said. "Were you expecting me?"

Salazar nodded. "For forty-one years."

Salazar served the coffee in mismatched cups, favoring only slightly his bandaged fingers.

Catching the direction of my glance, he said, "Company is worth a few burns, Ms. Sharma."

I accepted the steaming cup and somehow it very nearly slipped out of my hands. I made a last microsecond recovery.

The director nodded thoughtfully. "You're new here."

"First time," I said, sipping coffee. It was awful. He must have made a mistake with the preparation.

"You think the network failures I've been reporting for my people are false?"

"The home office has some suspicions of that," I admitted.

"I don't blame them, but they ain't. Look, the company gambles on probability, doesn't it?"

"No. It works on patterns calculated from network theory and past experience."

"But I mean it knows that there will be, say, a hundred network failures in a day. But it doesn't know if maybe ninety of them will be in one region and only ten in the rest of the country."

"There's something to that. We call it statistical distribution, not probability alone."

"Well, distribution says that more network failures are going to occur in Lakeside Village than anywhere else in the country, per capita."

I shook my head at Salazar. "That's not distribution. Theoretically, anything can happen but I don't—I can't—believe that in this village everybody has chanced to experience communication failures. Some other factor is operating. You are all deliberately sabotaging these connections—"

"We're not," Salazar snapped.

"Or else something is causing you to have this trouble. Maybe the whole village is using illegal jamming equipment. Maybe you manufacture your own interference devices; it's happened before."

Salazar laughed.

"Whatever is going on, I'm going to find it out. I don't care what you do, but if I can find a greater risk here and prove it, the Commission will let us discontinue service for this region. Probably beyond the capacity of these people to appeal, I'm afraid."

"That would be a real tragedy, Ms. Sharma. Communication is vital to this village. Nobody could survive a year here without reliable networks. People pay me for their service before they pay their utility bills."

I shrugged, sorrier than I could let on. "I won't be able to pay for my own utilities if I don't do the kind of job the company expects. I'm going to investigate."

"All right," he said grudgingly, "but you'll have to do it carefully."

"Yes, I understood you didn't like electronic vehicles on your paths. At least not the vehicles of outsiders."

"That doesn't have anything to do with it. Nobody in Lakeside Village owns an electronic vehicle. It would be system failure for anybody to use one, same as it would be to have wireless routers, instead of shielded cable, or to own quantum processors."

I took a deep breath.

"Optical systems," Salazar said. "With redundant backups and manual overrides."

I acknowledged his information. "You've been a great help."

"Four o'clock," he said. "Weather patterns are dangerous at night."

"There's always a dawn."

Salazar met my eyes. "That's not quite how we look at it here."

The mine was a mess.

I couldn't understand the way they extracted the crystal out of the mountain. The idea of random extraction—a completely unsystematic approach—going after a deposit of valuable crystal kept turning up in my mind as I walked around.

The workers were gone; it was after five local time. But here and there I saw traces of them. Some of them were equipment cases and tool marks, but most of the traces were signs of injury. Bandages left on sharp rocks, medical supplies scattered beneath heavy equipment, protective gear damaged on the handles and working surfaces of extraction tools and machinery. The place was as hazardous as a disaster zone.

"What are you looking for, miss?"

The low, level question had come from a sturdy woman in protective gear and a safety helmet.

"The reason you have so many network failures here," I said frankly. "I'm from the communications company. Name's Sharma."

"Yeah, I know."

I had supposed she would.

"I'm Jasmine Perry, the supervisor here," the woman told me, extending a work-worn hand to be shaken. "Outside, doing my training rotation, I noticed that most places don't have as many communication problems as we do here. Never could figure it out."

"This crystal is part of it—"

"What do you mean by that!" Perry demanded sharply.

"I mean the way you extract it. No system to it. No logical progression, no methodical approach..."

"Listen, Sharma, don't talk about what you don't know anything about. The material in these walls isn't just crystal; it isn't even ordinary quantum-grade material. Lakeside Village exports some of the finest grade of crystalline processors in the world. And it's used all over the world. We aren't just a bunch of unskilled laborers—we are specialists. We have to figure a different way of extracting every piece of crystal."

"It's too bad."

"What's too bad?"

"That you chose the wrong approach so often," I said.

Perry breathed frustration into my face. "Listen, Sharma, we have been working this mine for generations, sometimes more of us working than other times. Today most of us are working extracting the crystal. That's the way we like it. We don't want any outsider coming in and interfering with that."

"If this mine has anything to do with sabotaging Global-Meridian, I can tell you that I will do something about that!"

As soon as my words left my mouth, the sickening feeling hit me that I shouldn't have said that.

The general store was called a supply center, but it wasn't particularly well-supplied.

I took a seat at the small café counter and ordered a beverage, politely declining the young clerk's offer of a local specialty drink for an extra charge. The clerk had pulled her dark hair back in a practical braid, and she moved behind the counter with the same careful, deliberate motions I'd noticed in all the villagers.

Behind me were three small tables and one solitary booth. Two people somewhere between forty and sixty sat at the nearest table playing cards.

Over my drink I saw the old woman I had almost struck on the road. She approached the heavy-set person at the payment terminal.

"Hello, Doctor," the heavy person said. "What can we do for you?"

"I'd like to send a message," she said in an urgent voice.

"Sure, Doctor, I'll transmit it right away on the communication terminal as soon as I get a free moment."

"You're sure you can send it? Right away?"

"Positive. Five credits, Doctor."

The doctor fumbled in her pocket and produced a credit chip. She examined it thoughtfully.

"I suppose the message can wait," she said resignedly. "I believe I will purchase some food supplies instead."

"Why not get a meal, Doctor? Special today. Only five credits. And since you're such a regular customer I'll include a beverage and dessert for nothing."

"That's—kind of you," the old woman said awkwardly.

The proprietor shrugged. "A person has to eat."

The woman called "the doctor" came over and sat down two seats away, ignoring me. The clerk prepared her meal and served it.

I stayed with my beverage and my thoughts. Something about the clerk's dark braid reminded me of the records technician back at headquarters, and for a moment my mind wandered to all those hours in the archives. Different from the flight, I thought idly—Anna with her bright copper hair bringing me drinks, versus hours of dim holographic displays with the brunette technician fetching data modules.

More and more, I was coming to believe that Lakeside Village wasn't a job for a network analyst like myself but a sociological analyst. System sabotage is a structural flaw in a community, yes. But when the whole society is involved, distorted, you can't isolate the flaw. The whole village was material for a social scientist; let them figure out why otherwise decent citizens felt secure in conspiracy to defraud an honored corporation.

I didn't feel that I was defeated or that the trip had been a failure. I had merely established to my intuitive satisfaction that the job was not in my field.

I glanced at the old woman. The proprietor of the store knew her and evidently thought her harmless enough to feed.

"I think I can make it down the mountain before the weather changes," I called over to her. "You can come along if you like."

The young clerk behind the counter stared at me. I looked over and caught the calculating eyes of Carmen Nichols, the proprietor, too. Finally, the old doctor turned on her seat, her face pale and her eyes sad and resigned.

"I doubt very much if either of us will be leaving, Ms. Sharma," she said. "Now."

I took my beverage and the doctor her meal over to the single booth. We looked at each other across the table.

"I am Doctor Ava Obrien of the Institute for Advanced Studies," the doctor said. "I left on my research sabbatical six months ago. I have been here ever since."

I looked at her clothes. "You must not have been very well funded for a year's research, Doctor."

"I," she said, "have enough research credits with me to fund a small laboratory. Nobody in this village will process them for me."

"I can understand why you want to go somewhere where people are more cooperative in that case."

"They know the credits are valid. It's me they refuse to trust to leave this place. They think they can't let me go."

"I don't see any restraints on you," I remarked.

"Just because you can't see them," she growled, "doesn't mean they aren't there. Director Salazar has the only long-range communication terminal in the village. He has politely refused to let me use it. I'm a suspicious and undesirable character; he's under no obligation to give me communication privileges, he says. Nichols has the message service concession—the transmission terminal behind the payment station over there. She takes my messages but I never see her send them off. And I never get a reply."

"Unfriendly of them," I said conservatively. "But how can they stop you from packing your research materials and leaving?"

"Nichols has the only functional vehicle in town—a small transport, barely larger than a cargo hauler. She makes about one trip a week down into Pearlbrook for supplies and deliveries. She's been the only one in or out of Lakeside Village for six months."

It seemed incredible—more than that, unlikely, to me. "How about the crystal itself? How do they ship it out?"

"It's a controlled supply product, managed carefully," Doctor Obrien said. "They stockpile it and once a year the executive offices for the company back in Pearlbrook Town runs in a transport system up the side of the mountain to collect it. That won't be for another five months, as nearly as I can find out. I may not survive that long."

"How are you living?" I asked. "If they won't process your credits—"

"I do research assistance for people. They feed me, give me a little money sometimes."

"I can see why you want to leave with me," I said. "Haven't you ever thought of just walking out?"

"Forty miles down a steep mountain road? I'm an old woman, Ms. Sharma, and I've gotten even older since I came to Lakeside Village."

I nodded. "You have any credentials, any identification, to back this up?"

Wordlessly, she handed over her identification, research permits, enough documentation to have satisfied any security protocol.

"Okay," I said. "I'll accept your story for the moment. Now answer me the big question: Why are the good people of Lakeside Village doing this to you? By any chance, you wouldn't happen to know of a mass conspiracy they are perpetrating on Global-Meridian?"

"I know nothing of their business practices," Obrien said, "but I do know that they are absolutely neurologically impaired!"

"I admit I have met more capable groups of human beings in my time."

"No, understand me. These people are literally neurologically impaired—they are inferior to other human beings in specific ways."

"Look, I know discrimination is a problem but I can't go along with you on that."

"Sharma, understand me, I insist. Neurologically speaking, it is well known that certain populations suffer certain deficiencies due to environment, exposure, genetic factors. Some can't process certain stimuli, maintain certain cognitive functions, perform certain tasks. The people of Lakeside Village have the most unusual deficiency on record, I admit. Their neural synchronization has been impaired. They are completely devoid of any intuitive communication ability, any unconscious information processing."

"Because they aren't telepaths, that doesn't mean that they are impaired," I protested. "I don't have any telepathic abilities either."

"But you do!" Obrien said earnestly. "Everybody has some neural synchronization ability, but we don't realize it. We don't have the fabulous abilities of a few recorded cases of natural telepaths, but we have some, a trace. Lakeside Village citizens have no neural synchronization ability whatsoever, not even the little that you and I and the rest of the world have!"

"You said you were from the Institute, didn't you?" I mused. "Maybe you know what you are talking about; I've never been sure. But these people can't suffer very much from their lack of what you call neural synchronization."

"I tell you they do," she said hoarsely. "We never realize it but we all have some power of unconscious prediction. If we didn't, we would have a hundred accidents a day—just as these people do. They can't anticipate the obstacle in the path the way we can, or that that particular tool will malfunction slightly. There are other things, as well. You'll find it is almost impossible to maintain extended communication with any of them—they have no telepathic ability, no matter how slight, to bridge the semantic gap. None of them can coordinate complex tasks. They don't have the unconscious neural ability to synchronize their actions. All of us can do that, even if the case of a true 'telepath' who can directly read thoughts is rare."

"Doctor, you mean these people are holding you here simply so you won't go out and tell the rest of the world that they are impaired?"

"They don't want the world to know why they are neurologically impaired," she said crisply. "It's the crystal! I don't understand why myself. I'm not a physicist or a genetic engineer. But for some reason the heavy concentration and particular pattern of the quantum resonance in its structure is responsible for both inhibiting the genes that transmit neural synchronization from generation to generation and affecting those abilities in the present generation. A kind of cognitive sterility."

"How do you know this?"

"We haven't the time for all that. But think about it. What else could it be? It's that crystal that they are shipping all over the world, spreading the contamination. I want to stop that contamination. To the people of Lakeside Village that means ruining their only industry, putting them all out of work. They are used to this neural impairment; they don't see anything so bad about it. Besides, like everybody else, they have some doubts that there really are such things as telepathy and neural synchronization to be affected."

"Frankly," I said, hedging only a little, "I don't know what to make of your story. This is something to be decided by somebody with authority—like the Director of Public Health or the President or Board Chairman of Global-Meridian. But the first thing to do is get you out of here. We had better get back to my vehicle. I've got good navigation systems to get down the mountain."

Obrien stood up eagerly, and knocked over her water glass, spilling liquid across the tabletop.

"Sorry," she said. "I should have been more careful of that. I try to stay away from the crystal as much as possible, but it's affecting me."

I should have remembered something then. But, naturally, I didn't.
